Rebates & incentives

What support actually exists — and what it depends on.

Australian solar and battery incentives are delivered through certificate schemes and state programs with their own rules. This page explains how they work, what decides eligibility, and where to verify the current position yourself.

Last reviewed: 15 October 2026Sources: official government and regulator pages

The mechanism

Incentives are certificates, applied as a discount.

Nothing is paid to you directly. An eligible installation creates certificates; their value is deducted from your invoice by the installer, who handles the paperwork. That is why the installer's documentation matters as much as the product.

Open — rules changed 1 May 2026Batteries

Cheaper Home Batteries Program

A federal program that reduces the upfront cost of an eligible home battery by issuing small-scale technology certificates (STCs) which the installer applies as a discount at the point of sale.

  • Support is applied as a discount on the invoice — you do not receive a cash payment or claim it yourself.
  • From 1 May 2026 the STC factor tapers by installed battery capacity, so a larger battery earns proportionally less support per kWh.
  • Rebates are determined by the installation date, not the date you sign a contract.
  • The battery must be installed with a solar PV system (new or existing) and product eligibility and installer requirements apply.
  • Retailers are required to provide accurate, current quotes — the regulator has publicly warned against quoting outdated prices.

Last verified 15 October 2026 · Clean Energy Regulator (Australian Government)

Clean Energy Regulator — Battery rebates are changing 1 May 2026
OpenSolar panels

Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (STCs for solar panels)

The long-running federal scheme that issues small-scale technology certificates for eligible solar panel systems. As with batteries, the value is normally passed on to you as a discount by the installer.

  • Certificate numbers depend on the system's zone rating, its capacity, and the remaining deeming period — which reduces each year and ends in 2030.
  • Because the deeming period shrinks annually, the support available for a given system size declines over time.
  • Eligible products and accredited installation are required.
  • The certificate market price varies, so two quotes for the same system size can include different discounts.

Last verified 15 October 2026 · Clean Energy Regulator (Australian Government)

Clean Energy Regulator — Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme
Varies by state — verify each programBoth

State and territory programs

Most states and territories run their own programs alongside the federal schemes. Eligibility tests, income caps, property requirements and funding rounds differ, and programs open and close without much notice.

  • Some programs are limited to owner-occupiers and include household income and property value tests.
  • Some are directed at specific groups such as rental properties, apartments, businesses or concession card holders.
  • Funding is often released in rounds, so a program can be open in one month and closed the next.
  • You may be able to combine state support with the federal schemes — but the program rules decide, not the installer.

Last verified 15 October 2026 · State and territory governments

Example: Solar Victoria program list (Victoria)

Reading a quote

Three things called discounts — only one is a government incentive.

Quotes happily blur them together. Each comes from a different place, carries different conditions, and deserves a different level of trust.

Government incentives

Certificate-based support under federal schemes — small-scale technology certificates for panels and batteries — plus any state or territory rebate that applies to your address. Rules, eligibility and values are set by the program administrators, applied as a point-of-sale discount by the installer, and limited by funding and dates.

Retailer discounts and offers

Price cuts, package deals, plan credits and "special offers" decided by the seller. They can be genuine value — but they are marketing, not entitlements. Check what the discount is subtracted from, whether conditions or expiry dates apply, and whether a cheaper headline price corresponds to a cheaper specification.

Financing arrangements

Loans, interest-free periods and payment plans offered by retailers, banks or state programs. Financing changes when you pay, not what you pay — interest, fees and the total cost belong in your comparison. It is not a rebate and should never be presented as one.

Ask for the arithmetic, in dollars

A trustworthy quote labels each element separately: system price, federal certificate discount with its current estimate, state support with its eligibility conditions, and the balance being financed. If a discount cannot be broken down, treat it as a marketing number until it can be.

Changed 1 May 2026

The federal battery support now tapers by capacity.

The Clean Energy Regulator publishes the taper as a set of capacity bands. Support per kWh is highest on the first band and reduces on larger systems:

  • First 0–14 kWh
    Full support on the first 14 kWh of capacity    STC factor at 100%
  • Above 14–28 kWh
    Support reduces on the next 14 kWh    STC factor at 60%
  • Above 28–50 kWh
    Support reduces further on the last band    STC factor at 15%

What this means for larger batteries

The authority publishes a solar battery STC calculator so you can estimate certificate numbers. The dollar value also depends on the market price of certificates at the time, which is why no responsible installer should quote a fixed discount without a current certificate estimate.

The regulator has also warned that rebates are determined by the installation date, not the contract date — and that retailers should not promise installations before a rule change unless the work can genuinely be completed in time.

State and territory programs

Support varies by jurisdiction — verify each one.

Programs open, close and change their values. Some were closed at the time of writing: Victoria's interest-free battery loan, for example, no longer accepts new applications, while the state's solar panel rebate remains available to eligible households. Eligibility

Six factors that decide most outcomes.

We can explain the rules and prepare documentation. We cannot decide your eligibility — that is the program administrator's role.

Who owns and lives in the property

Many programs are limited to owner-occupiers. Some include separate categories for rental properties, apartments or homes under construction, and several require the owner's consent in writing.

Household income and property value tests

Some state programs apply a combined household income cap and a property value threshold. These figures are set by the program and change periodically.

Program history at the address

An address that has already received support for the same technology is usually ineligible — which matters when you buy an existing home with a system already installed.

Products on the eligible list

Programs publish lists of approved panels, inverters and batteries. A product that is perfectly good but not on the list will not attract support.

Who installs it

Installation must generally be carried out by an accredited installer engaged through an approved or authorised retailer, with the correct documentation submitted afterwards.

Timing and compliance paperwork

Installation windows, proof of eligibility documents, photographic compliance requirements and grid pre-approvals all affect whether support is paid. Missing paperwork can mean losing it.

Where our estimate differs from an official figure

Numbers produced by this website — including battery support shown in the savings estimator — are indicative models with stated assumptions. They are not official calculations, and they are not a promise of value. The authority's own calculator and your installer's current quote are the references that matter.

Verify it yourself

Five checks, a few minutes, official sources only.

You do not have to take any provider's word for what is available — including ours. These are the sources we check, in the order we check them.

  1. Start federal

    Check the Clean Energy Regulator's Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme page and, for batteries, the notice on the 1 May 2026 changes. Those pages define how certificates are calculated and which date decides eligibility.

  2. Then your state or territory

    Open the official page for your jurisdiction from the directory table above. Look for whether the program is accepting applications, what income or property tests apply, and whether funding is released in rounds.

  3. Check the products

    Confirm every quoted panel, inverter and battery appears on the eligible product lists for the programs involved — the industry's approved products program is the usual starting point.

  4. Check the installer

    Verify accreditation status directly with Solar Accreditation Australia, and check whether the company operates under the New Energy Tech Consumer Code.

  5. Check the price side

    Use Energy Made Easy to confirm your plan's usage rates and feed-in tariff, so savings claims can be judged against your real prices rather than averages.

What could change next

Incentives are designed to decline over time.

  • The federal deeming period shortens each year until the scheme's scheduled end in 2030 — the same system earns fewer certificates the longer you wait.
  • Battery capacity factors are set by regulation and were adjusted once already (1 May 2026); they can be varied again.
  • State programs exhaust their funding rounds and close without much notice — Victoria's battery loan is a live example of a program that stopped accepting applications.
  • Certificate market prices float, so identical certificate volumes convert to different dollar discounts between two quotes on the same day.
  • Network export limits and connection rules change independently of any rebate — they decide what a system is allowed to do, not just what it earns.

So what should you do about it?

Get the incentive treatment written into the contract with an explicit "what happens if it changes" clause. Never sign specifically to beat a deadline you have not verified at the official source. And keep perspective: the discount is the smallest part of the decision — the specification and the installation quality outlive every rebate.

Application process

From research to invoice, in six steps.

  1. Confirm the current program rules

    Start at the official source for your jurisdiction — not a sales page. Check the current funding round, the income and property tests, and the eligible product list.

  2. Get a written quote that treats incentives honestly

    A quote should show the system price, the incentive treatment, and what happens if the incentive value changes between quoting and installation.

  3. Complete the pre-installation steps

    Some programs require pre-approval to connect and export, a portal application, or proof of income before work begins. Installing before approval can void support.

  4. Install within the required window

    Programs impose installation deadlines — Solar Victoria, for example, uses deadlines that differ for existing homes and homes under construction.

  5. Submit the documentation

    Certificates of electrical safety, compliance paperwork, photographs and product documentation are submitted after installation. Keep your own copies.

  6. Verify what was applied to your invoice

    Your final invoice should show the discount that was actually applied. If the incentive value changed, it should be explained in writing.

Before you sign

A short verification checklist

  • Confirm the program is currently accepting applications.
  • Check the products quoted appear on the eligible product list.
  • Confirm who holds the accreditation and licence for the work.
  • Ask what happens if the incentive value changes before installation.
  • Keep copies of every document submitted on your behalf.

How we handle incentives in a proposal

A Solvanta proposal separates the system price from the incentive treatment, states the assumptions used to value certificates, and documents what happens if the available support changes between quoting and installation.

Important disclaimers

  • We are not affiliated with, endorsed by, or acting for any government agency or program administrator.
  • Program rules, funding rounds and values change. The information here is a starting point verified on the date shown — confirm everything with the official source before making a decision.
  • No provider can guarantee that you will qualify for a program, or that a discount amount will still be available when your installation is completed.
  • Incentive support is usually applied by the installer as a discount on your invoice. Where support is reduced or unavailable for any reason, the difference is normally payable by the customer.
